notes:
1. Rabindranath Tagore — Overview

  • Rabindranath Tagore was a poet, novelist, dramatist, composer, essayist, philosopher, painter and educationist.
  • He was one of the greatest figures of the Bengal Renaissance.
  • He became the first Asian Nobel laureate in Literature.
  • His writings combined:
  • Humanism.
  • Spirituality.
  • Freedom.
  • Social criticism.
  • Internationalism.
  • He wrote the song that became India's National Anthem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabindranath Tagore → Gitanjali + Nobel Prize + Jana Gana Mana + Santiniketan

2. Birth

  • Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861.
  • He was born at Jorasanko in Calcutta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → 7 May 1861 → Jorasanko, Calcutta

3. Bengali Calendar

  • Tagore's birthday is traditionally celebrated in Bengal as Rabindra Jayanti.
  • It falls on the 25th day of the Bengali month of Baishakh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabindra Jayanti → 25 Baishakh

4. Jorasanko Thakur Bari

  • Tagore was born in the famous Tagore family residence known as Jorasanko Thakur Bari.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jorasanko Thakur Bari → Rabindranath Tagore

5. Father

  • Tagore's father was Debendranath Tagore.
  • Debendranath was an important leader of the Brahmo Samaj.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabindranath's Father → Debendranath Tagore

6. Mother

  • Tagore's mother was Sarada Devi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mother → Sarada Devi

7. Grandfather

  • Tagore's grandfather was Dwarkanath Tagore.
  • He was a wealthy entrepreneur and prominent figure of nineteenth-century Bengal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dwarkanath Tagore → Grandfather of Rabindranath

8. Tagore Family

The Tagore family contributed significantly to:

  • Literature.
  • Music.
  • Art.
  • Theatre.
  • Religious reform.
  • Social thought.

9. Brahmo Samaj Background

  • Rabindranath grew up in a family closely connected with the Brahmo Samaj.
  • This environment encouraged:
  • Religious reform.
  • Monotheism.
  • Intellectual inquiry.

10. Debendranath and Brahmo Samaj

  • Debendranath Tagore became one of the major leaders of the Brahmo movement after Raja Rammohan Roy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Debendranath Tagore → Brahmo Samaj

11. Tattvabodhini Sabha

  • Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tattvabodhini Sabha → Debendranath Tagore → 1839

12. Tagore's Childhood Education

  • Tagore disliked rigid classroom education.
  • Much of his learning took place through:
  • Private tutors.
  • Reading.
  • Music.
  • Nature.
  • Travel.

13. Early Literary Talent

  • Tagore began writing poetry at a very young age.
  • His talent became visible during adolescence.

14. Bhanusimha

  • As a young writer, Tagore used the pseudonym Bhanusimha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhanusimha → Rabindranath Tagore

15. Bhanusimha's Poems

  • Under the name Bhanusimha, Tagore composed poems imitating the style of medieval Vaishnava devotional lyrics.

16. England Journey

  • Tagore travelled to England in 1878.
  • His family hoped he would study law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → England → 1878

17. University College London

  • Tagore studied for a period at University College London.
  • He did not complete a formal law degree.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tagore Studied in England → Did Not Become a Practising Lawyer

18. Return to India

  • Tagore returned to India without completing formal legal training.
  • He increasingly devoted himself to:
  • Literature.
  • Music.
  • Social thought.

19. Marriage

  • Tagore married Mrinalini Devi in 1883.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore's Wife → Mrinalini Devi

20. Estate Management

  • During the 1890s Tagore spent considerable time managing family estates in eastern Bengal.

21. Shilaidaha

  • Shilaidaha became closely connected with Tagore's life and literary development.
  • It is now in Bangladesh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shilaidaha → Tagore's Estate Years

22. Rural Bengal

  • His direct contact with rural Bengal influenced his:
  • Short stories.
  • Social observations.
  • Rural-development ideas.

23. Bengal Countryside

  • Tagore travelled through villages and interacted with:
  • Peasants.
  • Local communities.
  • Rural workers.

24. Short-Story Development

  • Tagore became one of the pioneers of the modern Bengali short story.
📌 Must-Memorise

Modern Bengali Short Story → Rabindranath Tagore

25. The Postmaster

  • The Postmaster is one of Tagore's best-known short stories.
📌 Must-Memorise

The Postmaster → Tagore

26. Kabuliwala

  • Kabuliwala is another famous short story written by Tagore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kabuliwala → Rabindranath Tagore

27. Kabuliwala — Theme

  • The story explores:
  • Human affection.
  • Separation.
  • Parenthood.
  • Cross-cultural empathy.

28. Literature Across Genres

Tagore wrote:

  • Poetry.
  • Novels.
  • Short stories.
  • Plays.
  • Essays.
  • Songs.
  • Letters.

29. Rabindra Sangeet

  • Tagore composed more than two thousand songs.
  • His musical tradition is known as Rabindra Sangeet.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabindra Sangeet → Songs of Rabindranath Tagore

30. Nature of Rabindra Sangeet

Rabindra Sangeet draws from several traditions including:

  • Bengali folk music.
  • Baul music.
  • Classical Indian music.
  • Devotional traditions.
  • Western musical influences.

31. Baul Influence

  • Tagore was deeply influenced by Bengal's Baul singers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baul Tradition → Important Influence on Tagore

32. Bauls

  • Bauls are wandering mystical singers associated especially with Bengal.
  • Their songs emphasise:
  • Inner spiritual experience.
  • Human unity.
  • Simplicity.

33. Lalon Fakir

  • The songs and ideas associated with Lalon Fakir formed part of the wider Baul cultural environment that influenced Tagore.

34. Early Poetry Collections

Important early poetry collections included works such as:

  • Sandhya Sangeet.
  • Manasi.
  • Sonar Tari.

35. Manasi

  • Manasi is an important collection in Tagore's development as a mature poet.

36. Sonar Tari

  • Sonar Tari means broadly "The Golden Boat."
📌 Must-Memorise

Sonar Tari → Tagore

37. Gitanjali

  • Gitanjali became Tagore's most internationally famous poetic work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gitanjali → Rabindranath Tagore

38. Meaning of Gitanjali

  • Gitanjali means approximately "Song Offerings."
📌 Must-Memorise

Gitanjali → Song Offerings

39. Bengali Gitanjali

  • The Bengali collection Gitanjali was published in 1910.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gitanjali → 1910

40. English Gitanjali

  • Tagore later translated a selection of his Bengali poems into English.
  • The English collection became widely known as Gitanjali: Song Offerings.

41. England — 1912

  • Tagore travelled to England in 1912 carrying English translations of his poems.

42. W.B. Yeats

  • Irish poet W.B. Yeats strongly admired Tagore's poetry.
  • Yeats wrote an introduction to the English edition of Gitanjali.
📌 Must-Memorise

W.B. Yeats → Introduction to English Gitanjali

43. International Recognition

  • Gitanjali brought Tagore extraordinary international literary recognition.

44. Nobel Prize

  • Rabindranath Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → Nobel Prize in Literature → 1913

45. First Asian Nobel Laureate

  • Tagore became the first Asian to receive a Nobel Prize.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Asian Nobel Laureate → Rabindranath Tagore

46. Nobel Field

  • His Nobel Prize was for Literature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tagore → Nobel Literature, Not Peace Prize

47. Nobel and Gitanjali

  • His international poetic reputation, especially associated with Gitanjali, was central to the Nobel recognition.

48. Nobel Importance

  • The award brought global attention to:
  • Indian literature.
  • Bengali culture.
  • Tagore's philosophical poetry.

49. "Where the Mind Is Without Fear"

  • One of Tagore's most famous poems expresses the hope for a society characterised by:
  • Freedom.
  • Knowledge.
  • Reason.
  • Fearlessness.
📌 Must-Memorise

"Where the Mind Is Without Fear" → Gitanjali / Tagore

50. Nationalism and Freedom

  • Tagore valued political freedom but argued that genuine freedom also required:
  • Intellectual freedom.
  • Moral freedom.
  • Human dignity.

51. Partition of Bengal

  • Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905.
  • Tagore participated actively in the early anti-partition movement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → Anti-Partition of Bengal Movement → 1905

52. Swadeshi Movement

  • Tagore initially supported Swadeshi mobilisation against the Partition of Bengal.

53. Raksha Bandhan

  • Tagore encouraged the use of Raksha Bandhan ceremonies to symbolise unity between different religious communities during the anti-partition movement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raksha Bandhan in Bengal Anti-Partition Movement → Tagore

54. Hindu-Muslim Unity

  • Tagore used the Raksha Bandhan symbolism to emphasise social unity rather than communal division.

55. Banglar Mati Banglar Jol

  • Tagore wrote patriotic songs associated with the anti-partition movement.
  • Banglar Mati Banglar Jol became one such important composition.

56. Amar Sonar Bangla

  • Tagore wrote Amar Sonar Bangla during the anti-partition movement of 1905.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amar Sonar Bangla → Tagore → 1905

57. Bangladesh National Anthem

  • The opening portion of Amar Sonar Bangla later became the National Anthem of Bangladesh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bangladesh National Anthem → Amar Sonar Bangla → Tagore

58. Ekla Chalo Re

  • Tagore composed the famous song Ekla Chalo Re.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ekla Chalo Re → Rabindranath Tagore

59. Meaning of Ekla Chalo Re

  • Its central message is to continue one's moral path even without support from others.

60. Gandhi and Ekla Chalo Re

  • The song became widely admired in nationalist circles, including by Mahatma Gandhi.

61. Tagore's Criticism of Swadeshi Excesses

  • Tagore became critical of:
  • Coercive boycott.
  • Aggressive nationalism.
  • Communal hostility.
  • He insisted that nationalism should not destroy human freedom.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Tagore Supported Freedom → But Criticised Aggressive Nationalism

62. Ghare-Baire

  • Tagore's novel Ghare-Baire, or The Home and the World, examines the Swadeshi movement and the dangers of aggressive nationalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ghare-Baire → Swadeshi + Nationalism Debate

63. Ghare-Baire Characters

The novel centres on characters including:

  • Nikhil.
  • Bimala.
  • Sandip.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sandip → Aggressive Nationalism

Nikhil → Ethical Humanism

64. Gora

  • Gora is one of Tagore's major novels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gora → Rabindranath Tagore

65. Themes of Gora

Gora examines:

  • Religion.
  • Caste.
  • Identity.
  • Nationalism.
  • Indian society.

66. Chokher Bali

  • Chokher Bali is another important Tagore novel.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chokher Bali → Tagore

67. Chokher Bali — Social Theme

  • It explores:
  • Widowhood.
  • Desire.
  • Social convention.
  • Women's position.

68. Jogajog

  • Jogajog is another major Tagore novel dealing with family and social relations.

69. Char Adhyay

  • Char Adhyay examines revolutionary nationalism and its moral consequences.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Char Adhyay → Revolutionary Politics Critique

70. Tagore as Social Critic

His fiction often examined:

  • Caste.
  • Gender.
  • Marriage.
  • Nationalism.
  • Social hypocrisy.
  • Individual freedom.

71. Women in Tagore's Literature

  • Tagore created complex female characters who questioned restrictive social conventions.

72. Tagore's Drama

Important dramatic works include:

  • Dak Ghar.
  • Raktakarabi.
  • Mukta Dhara.
  • Chitrangada.

73. Dak Ghar

  • Dak Ghar is known in English as The Post Office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dak Ghar → The Post Office → Tagore

74. The Post Office — Theme

  • The play explores:
  • Freedom.
  • Imagination.
  • Liberation from confinement.

75. Raktakarabi

  • Raktakarabi is often translated as Red Oleanders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raktakarabi → Red Oleanders

76. Raktakarabi — Theme

  • It critiques:
  • Greed.
  • Mechanised exploitation.
  • Dehumanising power.

77. Mukta Dhara

  • Mukta Dhara is another major symbolic play by Tagore.

78. Chitrangada

  • Chitrangada was inspired by the Mahabharata character Chitrangada.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chitrangada → Tagore → Mahabharata Inspiration

79. Dance Drama

  • Tagore helped develop a distinctive Bengali dance-drama tradition through works such as:
  • Chitrangada.
  • Chandalika.
  • Shyama.

80. Chandalika

  • Chandalika addresses:
  • Caste.
  • Human dignity.
  • Social exclusion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandalika → Anti-Caste / Human Dignity Theme

81. Buddhist Influence

  • Chandalika draws upon a Buddhist narrative.

82. Shyama

  • Shyama is another famous Tagore dance-drama.

83. Tagore and Music

  • Tagore wrote both words and melodies for a vast body of songs.
  • Music was central to his educational and cultural philosophy.

84. Jana Gana Mana

  • Tagore composed Jana Gana Mana.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jana Gana Mana → Rabindranath Tagore

85. First Public Performance

  • Jana Gana Mana was first publicly sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in December 1911.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jana Gana Mana → Calcutta INC Session → 1911

86. Language

  • The original song was composed in a highly Sanskritised form of Bengali.

87. National Anthem

  • The Constituent Assembly adopted Jana Gana Mana as India's National Anthem on 24 January 1950.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Anthem Adopted → 24 January 1950

88. National Anthem vs National Song

⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

National Anthem → Jana Gana Mana → Tagore

National Song → Vande Mataram → Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay

89. Vande Mataram

  • Vande Mataram appeared in Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath.

90. Tagore and Vande Mataram

  • Tagore sang Vande Mataram at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore Sang Vande Mataram at INC → 1896

91. Two National Anthems

Tagore's songs became national anthems of:

  • India → Jana Gana Mana.
  • Bangladesh → Amar Sonar Bangla.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → National Anthems of India + Bangladesh

92. Santiniketan

  • Santiniketan became the centre of Tagore's educational experiments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santiniketan → Rabindranath Tagore

93. Santiniketan Origin

  • Tagore's father Debendranath had earlier established a spiritual retreat at Santiniketan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Debendranath → Original Santiniketan Retreat

Rabindranath → Educational Institution

94. School at Santiniketan

  • Rabindranath Tagore established a school at Santiniketan in 1901.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santiniketan School → 1901 → Tagore

95. Brahmacharyashrama

  • The early school was associated with the name Brahmacharyashrama.

96. Educational Philosophy

Tagore opposed:

  • Rote learning.
  • Excessively rigid classrooms.
  • Mechanical examinations.

He favoured:

  • Freedom.
  • Creativity.
  • Nature.
  • Arts.
  • International understanding.

97. Open-Air Education

  • Classes at Santiniketan were often held in natural surroundings.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore Education → Nature + Open-Air Learning

98. Role of Arts

Education at Santiniketan integrated:

  • Music.
  • Painting.
  • Drama.
  • Literature.
  • Crafts.

99. Teacher–Student Relationship

  • Tagore preferred close, personal interaction between teachers and students.

100. International Education

  • Tagore wanted Santiniketan to become a meeting place for different civilisations.

101. Visva-Bharati

  • Tagore founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Visva-Bharati → Rabindranath Tagore

102. Visva-Bharati — Year

  • Visva-Bharati formally developed as a university-level institution in 1921.
📌 Must-Memorise

Visva-Bharati → 1921

103. Meaning of Visva-Bharati

  • Its ideal was to bring India into intellectual dialogue with the wider world.

104. Motto

  • Visva-Bharati's motto draws from a Sanskrit expression meaning broadly that the whole world meets in one nest.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Visva-Bharati → International Cultural Meeting Place

105. World University Idea

  • Tagore envisioned Visva-Bharati as an institution transcending narrow national boundaries.

106. Sriniketan

  • Tagore established a rural-reconstruction centre at Sriniketan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sriniketan → Rural Reconstruction

107. Sriniketan — Year

  • Sriniketan developed from 1922 as a major rural-reconstruction initiative.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sriniketan → 1922

108. Leonard Elmhirst

  • English agricultural economist Leonard K. Elmhirst worked with Tagore in developing Sriniketan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Leonard Elmhirst → Sriniketan

109. Rural Reconstruction

Sriniketan focused on:

  • Agriculture.
  • Rural education.
  • Cooperative work.
  • Health.
  • Crafts.
  • Village self-help.

110. Tagore and Villages

  • Tagore believed India's national regeneration required improvement of rural society, not merely political agitation.

111. Cooperatives

  • He encouraged cooperative economic methods in rural areas.

112. Education and Rural Development

  • Tagore linked education with practical rural improvement.

113. Gandhi and Tagore

  • Gandhi and Tagore had a relationship of mutual respect.
  • They also debated several political and philosophical issues.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi + Tagore → Mutual Respect + Intellectual Debate

114. Gurudev

  • Gandhi frequently addressed Tagore as Gurudev.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gurudev → Rabindranath Tagore

115. Mahatma

  • Tagore also used the honorific Mahatma for Gandhi.
  • Claims about the exact first use of the title should be treated cautiously.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

"Who First Called Gandhi Mahatma?" → Historically Disputed

116. Gandhi–Tagore Debates

They differed on issues including:

  • Non-Cooperation.
  • Nationalism.
  • Charkha.
  • Modernity.
  • Education.

117. Shared Values

Despite disagreements, both valued:

  • Human dignity.
  • Rural uplift.
  • Moral politics.
  • Indian freedom.

118. Tagore and Non-Cooperation

  • Tagore was critical of aspects of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • He feared that negative boycott and narrow nationalism could restrict intellectual freedom.

119. Gandhi's Response

  • Gandhi defended Non-Cooperation as a moral withdrawal from unjust rule.
  • Their exchange became one of modern India's important intellectual debates.

120. Charkha Debate

  • Tagore respected rural reconstruction but questioned making the spinning wheel a universal symbol of national regeneration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gandhi–Tagore Debate → Charkha + Nationalism + Education

121. Tagore's Nationalism

  • Tagore opposed colonial domination.
  • But he also criticised aggressive nation-state nationalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → Anti-Colonial, Yet Critical of Aggressive Nationalism

122. Nationalism Lectures

  • Tagore delivered lectures on nationalism in countries including Japan and the United States during the 1910s.

123. Nationalism — Book

  • His lectures were published in a work titled Nationalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nationalism → Rabindranath Tagore

124. Critique of Western Nationalism

  • Tagore criticised nationalism when it became:
  • Militaristic.
  • Imperialist.
  • Mechanically organised.
  • Hostile to humanity.

125. Universal Humanism

  • Tagore placed humanity above narrow national identity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore's Philosophy → Universal Humanism

126. Internationalism

  • Tagore believed cultures should learn from one another without losing their individuality.

127. East-West Dialogue

  • He sought meaningful dialogue between:
  • Indian civilisation.
  • Western knowledge.
  • Asian cultures.

128. Japan

  • Tagore visited Japan several times.
  • He admired elements of Japanese culture while warning against militaristic nationalism.

129. China

  • Tagore visited China and encouraged Asian cultural dialogue.

130. Europe and America

  • Tagore travelled extensively in Europe and the United States.

131. Soviet Union

  • Tagore visited the Soviet Union in 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → Soviet Union Visit → 1930

132. Letters from Russia

  • Tagore wrote observations about his Soviet visit, later known through Letters from Russia.
📌 Must-Memorise

Letters from Russia → Tagore

133. Soviet Education

  • Tagore admired aspects of:
  • Mass education.
  • Literacy.
  • He nevertheless remained wary of excessive political conformity.

134. Albert Einstein

  • Tagore met physicist Albert Einstein.
  • Their conversations explored:
  • Truth.
  • Reality.
  • Science.
  • Human consciousness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore + Einstein → Famous Intellectual Conversations

135. Romain Rolland

  • Tagore maintained intellectual connections with European writers and thinkers such as Romain Rolland.

136. W.B. Yeats

  • Yeats played a major role in introducing Tagore's English poetry to European literary circles.

137. C.F. Andrews

  • Charles Freer Andrews was a close friend of Tagore and Gandhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

C.F. Andrews → Friend of Tagore and Gandhi

138. Deenabandhu Andrews

  • C.F. Andrews became popularly known in India as Deenabandhu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deenabandhu → C.F. Andrews

139. Knighthood

  • The British Crown conferred a knighthood on Rabindranath Tagore in 1915.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore Knighted → 1915

140. Jallianwala Bagh

  • British troops fired on an unarmed gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, on 13 April 1919.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jallianwala Bagh → 13 April 1919

141. Tagore's Protest

  • Tagore strongly condemned the massacre.

142. Renunciation of Knighthood

  • Tagore renounced his knighthood in 1919 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore Renounced Knighthood → 1919 → Jallianwala Bagh

143. Letter to Viceroy

  • Tagore communicated his renunciation to Viceroy Lord Chelmsford.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore's Renunciation Letter → Lord Chelmsford

144. Significance

  • Returning the honour became a powerful symbolic act of moral protest against British rule.

145. Tagore vs Gandhi — British Honours

  • Tagore renounced his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh.
  • Gandhi later returned British honours during the Non-Cooperation phase.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tagore → Knighthood Renounced

Gandhi → Returned Medals/Honours

146. Tagore and Colonialism

  • Tagore consistently criticised:
  • Racial arrogance.
  • Imperial exploitation.
  • Cultural domination.

147. Anti-Colonialism vs Nationalism

  • Tagore's opposition to aggressive nationalism did not mean support for colonialism.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Critic of Nationalism ≠ Supporter of British Rule

148. Nobel Prize and Knighthood Sequence

  • 1913 → Nobel Prize.
  • 1915 → Knighthood.
  • 1919 → Knighthood renounced.
📌 Must-Memorise

1913 → Nobel

1915 → Knighted

1919 → Renounced

149. Tagore as Painter

  • Tagore began painting seriously relatively late in life.
  • He nevertheless developed a distinctive modern artistic style.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tagore → Poet + Painter

150. Art Style

His visual art included:

  • Faces.
  • Imaginary creatures.
  • Landscapes.
  • Abstract forms.

151. International Art Exhibitions

  • Tagore's paintings were exhibited internationally during his later years.

152. Kala Bhavana

  • Visva-Bharati's Kala Bhavana became an important centre for modern Indian art.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kala Bhavana → Visva-Bharati → Art

153. Nandalal Bose

  • Nandalal Bose became one of the most important artists associated with Kala Bhavana.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nandalal Bose → Kala Bhavana

154. Benode Behari Mukherjee

  • Benode Behari Mukherjee was another major artist associated with Santiniketan.

155. Ramkinkar Baij

  • Sculptor Ramkinkar Baij became an important figure of the Santiniketan art tradition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ramkinkar Baij → Santiniketan Sculpture

156. Santiniketan Art School

  • The Santiniketan environment encouraged modern Indian art rooted in indigenous traditions while remaining open to global influences.

157. Sangeet Bhavana

  • Music and performing arts became integral parts of Visva-Bharati's educational system.

158. Cheena Bhavana

  • Visva-Bharati developed centres devoted to Asian cultural studies, including Chinese studies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Visva-Bharati → International/Asian Studies

159. Hindi Bhavana

  • Institutions studying Indian languages and cultures also developed at Santiniketan.

160. Tagore and Education — Central Principle

For Tagore:

Education should develop:

  • Imagination.
  • Freedom.
  • Creativity.
  • Moral awareness.
  • Relationship with nature.

161. Opposition to Rote Learning

  • Tagore strongly criticised education based only on:
  • Memorisation.
  • Examinations.
  • Discipline imposed from above.

162. Mother Tongue

  • He valued education through the learner's cultural and linguistic environment.

163. World Culture

  • Tagore wanted students to learn about cultures beyond India as well.

164. Nature

  • Nature itself was treated as part of the classroom at Santiniketan.

165. Festivals at Santiniketan

  • Seasonal and cultural festivals were integrated into educational life.

166. Holistic Education

Tagore's model combined:

  • Intellectual study.
  • Arts.
  • Physical environment.
  • Community.
  • Practical activity.

167. Tagore and Rural Poverty

  • Direct experience of rural Bengal convinced Tagore that political freedom alone would not solve poverty.

168. Rural Credit

  • He experimented with cooperative and rural-credit initiatives on family estates.

169. Cooperative Principle

  • Tagore believed cooperation could help overcome rural isolation and indebtedness.

170. Agricultural Improvement

  • Sriniketan promoted improved agricultural knowledge and village development.

171. Tagore and Science

  • Tagore valued scientific inquiry and encouraged dialogue between:
  • Science.
  • Humanities.
  • Philosophy.
